Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
m=\left\lfloor \sqrt n\right\rfloor .
\]

We will determine which prime powers can divide \(n\).

Suppose \(p^a\mid n\).

---

### 1. If \(p\le m\)

Then \(p\mid m!\), so

\[
p\mid (m!)^{n!}.
\]

More strongly, since \(p^a\mid n\), we have \(p^a\le n\), and therefore

\[
v_p\bigl((m!)^{n!}\bigr)=n!v_p(m!)\ge n!\ge n\ge p^a\ge a.
\]

Thus \(p^a\mid (m!)^{n!}\). Hence for \(p^a\) to divide

\[
(m!)^{n!}+450,
\]

we must have

\[
p^a\mid 450.
\]

So any prime power of \(n\) coming from primes \(p\le m\) must divide

\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2.
\]

---

### 2. If \(p>m\)

Then \(p\nmid m!\). Also, since \(p\mid n\), we have \(p\le n\), so

\[
p-1\mid n!.
\]

By Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(m!)^{n!}\equiv 1 \pmod p.
\]

Therefore we need

\[
1+450=451\equiv 0\pmod p,
\]

so

\[
p\mid 451=11\cdot 41.
\]

Also, since \(p>m\), we have

\[
p^2\ge (m+1)^2>n,
\]

so \(p\) can appear only to the first power.

Thus the only possible prime factors of \(n\) are

\[
2,3,5,11,41,
\]

with exponents bounded by those in

\[
450\cdot 451=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2\cdot 11\cdot 41.
\]

---

### 3. Bounding \(n\)

If \(m\ge 41\), then both \(11\) and \(41\) are \(\le m\), so neither can divide \(n\). Thus \(n\mid 450\). But \(m\ge 41\) implies

\[
n\ge m^2\ge 41^2=1681,
\]

contradicting \(n\mid 450\). Hence

\[
m\le 40.
\]

If \(m\le 10\), then

\[
n<(m+1)^2\le 121,
\]

so \(n\le 120\), which is below our eventual maximum.

Now suppose

\[
11\le m\le 40.
\]

Then \(11\le m\), so \(11\nmid n\). Therefore

\[
n\mid 450\cdot 41.
\]

Also,

\[
n<(m+1)^2\le 41^2=1681,
\]

so \(n\le 1680\).

If \(41\nmid n\), then \(n\mid 450\), so \(n\le 450\).

If \(41\mid n\), write \(n=41d\), where \(d\mid 450\). Then

\[
41d\le 1680 \implies d\le 40.
\]

The largest divisor of \(450\) not exceeding \(40\) is \(30\). Hence

\[
n\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

So every admissible \(n\) satisfies

\[
n\le 1230.
\]

---

### 4. Check that \(n=1230\) works

We have

\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41
\]

and

\[
\left\lfloor \sqrt{1230}\right\rfloor =35,
\]

since \(35^2=1225<1230<1296=36^2\).

We check divisibility modulo each prime factor of \(1230\).

- Modulo \(2,3,5\):  
  \(35!\) is divisible by \(2,3,5\), so

  \[
  (35!)^{1230!}\equiv 0 \pmod p
  \]

  for \(p=2,3,5\). Also \(450\equiv 0\pmod p\). Thus the sum is divisible by \(p\).

- Modulo \(41\):  
  \(35!\) is not divisible by \(41\). Since \(40\mid 1230!\), Fermat’s little theorem gives

  \[
  (35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1 \pmod{41}.
  \]

  Therefore

  \[
  (35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1+450=451\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
  \]

Thus \(1230\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450\).

Hence the largest possible \(n\) is

\[
\boxed{1230}.
\]
